top_comments: > When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.Wish I had this restraint. I’ve been vibing everything I can think of. It’s got to the point I made a small platform on top of k3s so that the agent can yolo deploy into a homeserver behind Tailscale. Once deployed it becomes natural selection for which vibes live and which die.Solo vibey self hosting llm usage - bliss.Corporate agentic engineering working with others - soul crushing.

In some ways it's better, in some ways it's worse.It's certainly easier than ever to spin up a VPS/cloudflare proxy and deploy. Agents can pretty much do that end to end.The bigger issue is you're then accountable for keeping up with security. Previously that meant using fail2ban and running a system update every few months. Now it means patching within 24hrs of a CVE9+ dropping, which is happening at an accelerated rate.It got so bad during October I made https://firefighter.sh/ as a joke (a root-permissioned agent that continuously monitors for CVEs and patches your system live as soon as they drop - it's a security nightmare given the nondeterministic aspect of AI), but I'm actually starting to come around to the idea for my non-critical servers.

With AI, the problem-solving aspect of my interest in computers is gone. And with it, much of my interest in computers.The fact that AI can do pretty much anything is amazing, but using it feels about as rewarding as using cheat codes in your favorite game as a kid.It's great fun for a while, until you realize you've ruined the game for yourself.

articles.title: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad
articles.summary: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad

top_comments: As a Westerner, I've been to Lahore, and the historical architecture is indeed fascinating. There are palaces and public buildings from the mughal period that would have been wonders of the world, had they still been standing. Only thing is, they are ruins, and you have to extrapolate from the few surviving pieces to the ruined whole to get an idea about the original splendor.Besides that, even though people there are very sweet, Lahore is not an international tourist city, so I don't know that I would recommend going, unless you know what you're getting into.

Thanks for showing this man's life's work. It's pretty obvious that he has spent his time and energy well. Preserving the ancient traditions is awesome too. Those examples in the article are simply beautiful, some in their complexity and others in their simplicity.From the land of stick-built structures and evenly distributed, look-alike strip malls. Pakistan looks beautiful.

Hear me out: there are hints of brutalism in his work. He trained at the AA in the early 60s, when New Brutalism was big in London, and his early buildings were modernist. To me the heavy massing and honesty about materials carried over, even though his later work brings back the ornament brutalism threw out.

articles.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
articles.summary: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad

top_comments: Author assumes price cartels, but this can be completely explained by supply and demand. Hyperscalars are buying all the storage they can get their hands on; that's it. Manufacturers are loath to ramp up supply (high CapEx), because they'll be underwater if the AI demand evaporates.

Memory, both chips and HDs, eventually collapses in price; that’s been the cycle for decades. The boom-and-bust cycle is what has driven the number of manufacturers down. My suspicion is that, in a few years, the price per gig will collapse again. AI is memory-hungry, and PC manufacturers will be pushing self-hosted AI models, which will require lots of memory. I bet we’ll see an increase in density per unit, which will bring down the price per gig. I give it five years at most. At that time, we will be seeing PC's capable of hosting a full AI model for the equivalen of less that $1000 today. It's how tech has worked for decades. There's no reason to think things have changed.

Yeah, this mirrors exactly what I have experienced in Australia.I started a business in 2023-2024 that needs a lot of storage (petabytes) and gosh that's really hurt our ability to sacle things. SSD'd were hit first, so we were a bit ahead of the curve and bought 20 packs of HDD's. That definitely kept us going. But I don't know if we can do more than another year at this kind of pricing.

In all seriousness, a related way I’ve observed culture differences in tech companies is in the presence, or lack thereof, of slack channels for random non work topicsAt one company i worked there were dozens of slack channels for just talking about sports to tv shows to pets and more; and very active. To the point where I genuinely questioned how some people could be so active at risk of the perception that would leave for ability to get actual work doneAnd at my current company, sure there’s a #pets channel but probably gets one post every 6 months.And if you’re curious, yes the company with less non-work slacks is the (far more) successful one.

It feels like you could extend this in another direction, and measure culture within a team/org by the amount & variety of emoji reactions to messages (on average).The best teams I've been on would have incredibly high response rate % average.In contrast, when I see an announcement go out to an 800 person org and all it gets is 4 generic emojis, the silence feels deafening (at least in my mind).
Side note: Teams also has custom emojis. See https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/teams-custo...

articles.summary: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' indicted for wire fraud

top_comments: Initially he only included a 2% margin - $260 over the around $13,000 requested by the fake ransomware group as the lowest possible price. And that $260 might have been just to account for bitcoin volatility.Only after this was comminicated to the fake victim, the fake ransomware group agreed to reduce the price. What should have he done, tell the customer that his yesterday's quote was a mistake?As for the initial $2,750 diagnostic fee, why can't he charge that, he did perform some initial study of the case.> The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.> The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

That's an interesting case. It's not immediately clear to me that this even is wire fraud. There is material deception (they claim "We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients", while paying ransom). But is there intent to defraud here? The customer does get what they asked for after all: they get their data back, at the price they were willing to payThat that price was substantially higher than what the ransomware groups were charging RansomwareHelp seems inconsequential, every business has markups. And RansomwareHelp might have been able to get substantial discounts by being a trusted repeat customer for those ransomware groups

I wonder if you could write the contracts so it isn't fraud? Just put "let us do whatever we need to do, including paying the ransom" in the contracts, and tell people that's just a break-glass that will not normally be needed.Because the way it's described, it definitely seems like fraud to market the thing as "won't pay the ransom" when you actually just do that.

articles.title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language
articles.summary: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language

top_comments: "Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it." — Donald KnuthFormal correctness does not guarantee desired function. People have written TLA+ specs for their software[1] and not have it materially improve the quality or reliability. You cannot just throw formal verification at a problem.I am very much of the opinion that crap code is an issue of organisation and aesthetics, and that can be automated. This is something that is enforced by frameworks, and despite the popular consensus that LLMs are good at frameworks because of training data, I make another argument that LLMs are good at them because frameworks massively restrict the possibility space of code that can exist and enforce a consistent organisation and aesthetic. The solution as I see it is to make more restrictive frameworks that have a higher chance of producing desired functionality, then afterward we can worry about correctness.[1] https://jepsen.io/analyses/particledb-1.1.4

Wow, I feel like Blaine is describe a language a lot like the one I'm working on now, Zena: https://zena-lang.dev/I started Zena from wanting a TypeScript-like syntax that compiled to very efficient WebAssembly GC, and AssemblyScript had issues...The motivation for targeting Wasm was as a good sandboxing and orchestration unit for AI-generated code. So, out of both general PL curiosity and enthusiasm, and an attempt to make a language that's good for AI generation, I started adding what I thought were the best features from other languages with a lot of focus on correctness, structure, and optimizability: pattern matching with exhaustiveness checking, ADTs and sum types via sealed classes, value types, async cancelation / structured concurrency, ownership and borrow checking for resources, unicode safe strings, and recently I added runtime contracts and I'll start on refinement types and some kind of proof system soon.The idea is exactly to take a mainstream and familiar-looking language and add more cutting-edge and academic features that help with software correctness.I wrote about some of this here, though not the formal methods parts: https://zena-lang.dev/blog/2026/09/languages-for-the-ai-era/

Dafny, SPARK Ada, Why3, Verus, Frama-C, TLA+, etc. are all sort of in this direction for different languages and styles of verification. It is nice to see them getting attention now that LLMs make them digestible for a broader set of programmers. I'm not sure one can start with a goal of creating a "mainstream" language that is verification-oriented. Mainstreamness comes from adoption. I'd look at those past languages (like the ones I listed), and ask "why did these not go mainstream" or "why did they not see broad adoption", and try some new ideas to address their gaps to see if a new one will catch on. But the "mainstream" part seems backwards as the goal - if it’s verifiable, ergonomic, flexible, and accessible, maybe it will go mainstream.
